## Summary

::: {.verdict}
**Verdict: major concerns.** The recommendation that "cognitive screening could be valuable" is
**not supported** by the reported counts.
The Kaplan–Meier figure cannot have been drawn from the data behind Table 2, and its own numbers at
risk place most events in the last ten weeks of follow-up. The follow-up dates do not allow the
median follow-up reported, so the time origin is unknown. The headline model adjusts for a variable
missing in about 29 % of the sample without saying so. The adjusted hazard ratio of about 2.5 rests
on 15 events in the exposed group and on an age effect the paper does not report; with an age
effect of the size commonly reported for stroke, the interval includes 1. The MMSE flags 15 of the
81 people who went on to an ischaemic stroke. What the reported numbers do support is that the
group with MMSE < 24, eleven years older at the median, had about four times the event rate.
:::

## What the paper does

A secondary analysis of the APAC community cohort: 5440 adults aged 40 or
older, free of stroke, transient ischaemic attack and coronary disease at the 2010/2011 baseline,
when risk factors and vascular imaging were collected. The Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) was
administered once, "in the first follow-up examination conducted in 2012/2013". After excluding
1512 participants without an MMSE and
53 with stroke or cardiovascular disease before that visit,
3875 were analysed; 192 (5\.0 %) had an MMSE
below 24, "defined as cognitive impairment in the present study". Outcomes were a first ischaemic
stroke, any first stroke and death from any cause, followed "until December 31, 2015", over "a
median follow-up of 4.1 years".

Analysis as described: Cox proportional-hazards models, unadjusted, adjusted for "age, gender, and
education" (Model 1), and with "additional adjustments for homocysteine levels, ICAS, hypertension,
and occupation" (Model 2); "Covariates were selected based on their established association with
stroke risk and their imbalance between groups in baseline comparisons." "The Kaplan-Meier method
and log-rank test were utilized to estimate the cumulative incidence". The paper's Table 2:

The conclusion: cognitive impairment "independently forecasted the occurrence of ischemic stroke

## Design

**The follow-up cannot run as stated.** The MMSE was measured in 2012/2013 and follow-up ended on
2015-12-31. Counted from the MMSE visit, follow-up lasts between 2\.0 and
4\.0 years. The paper reports a median of 4\.1
years, and the numbers at risk under Figure 2 show 99\.2 % and
96\.9 % of the two groups still under observation at year 4.

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
A median of 4.1 years and four years of observation for nearly everyone are possible only if time
starts at the 2010/2011 baseline. In that case the exposure was measured about two years after
time zero, every analysed participant was alive and stroke-free for those two years by
construction, and the deaths that Figure 2 shows in the first year belong to people who could not
have taken the MMSE in 2012/2013. The paper does not state the time origin. Which of the two holds
needs the visit and event dates.
:::

**"Baseline" names two visits two years apart.** Covariates and vascular imaging date from
2010/2011, the exposure from 2012/2013. Table 1 gives a median age of 51\.6
and the Discussion a "relatively young baseline age (median: 53\.4 years)".

::: {.evidence-inferred}
The two-year gap between the two medians suggests that the covariates in the models are the
2010/2011 values: hypertension, homocysteine and stenosis status measured two years before the
exposure adjust a comparison defined at the later visit.
:::

**A quarter of the cohort is excluded for a missing exposure.** 1512 of
5440 (27\.8 %) had no
MMSE. By Supplementary Table S1 the excluded were older and more often male, hypertensive, diabetic
and with intracranial stenosis. No reason for the missing MMSE is given, and no weighting or
imputation is used. The Discussion holds that selection bias was handled because "we have adjusted
for these factors in our models".

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
Adjusting within the included sample says nothing about the excluded one. The excluded part is the
part with more vascular disease, where low MMSE scores are most common; the estimates apply to a
selected sample, and the paper reads them as for stroke-free adults aged 40 and over.
:::

**Loss to follow-up is never reported.** For "those participants who missed the follow-up exams,
outcome data was gathered by reviewing death certificates ..., discharge summaries from the 11
hospitals, and medical records". How many missed an exam is not stated, and nobody is described as
censored before the end of 2015. By the numbers at risk of the mortality panel,
30 of 3683 and
6 of 192
participants left the risk set for any reason, deaths included, in four years.

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
A participant who missed the exams counts as event-free unless a record is found. Deaths are found
through vital statistics; a non-fatal stroke treated outside the 11 hospitals is not. Ascertainment
therefore differs between attenders and non-attenders and between stroke and death, in a direction
the paper gives no means to judge, and with 15 exposed events a handful of missed strokes matters.
The re-analysis below takes the paper at its word on this point.
:::

## Measurement

**The exposure is one MMSE below a fixed cut-off.** 93
of the 192 participants classed as impaired
(48\.4 %) have primary schooling or less, against
8\.2 % of the others. No education-specific
cut-off, second instrument or repeat test is used, and the continuous score, with a median of
29, enters no analysis. The authors mention "potential educational bias".

::: {.evidence-inferred}
Part of what the exposure measures is schooling. The title's claim is about cognitive impairment;
the data cannot separate the two without the continuous score and an education-stratified analysis.
:::

**A Model 2 covariate is missing for about 29 % of the sample.** Table 1 prints manual work as
2009 participants (51\.9 %).
Supplementary Table S1 prints the same 2009 as 73\.3 %, which is a
fraction of 2739 to 2742 people, not of
3875.

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
Occupation is recorded for about 71 % of the analysed sample.
A Cox model in SAS drops records with a missing covariate, so Model 2, the model of the abstract,
is fitted on at most about 2742 participants and on an unknown number of the
events of Table 2. The paper presents Models 1 and 2 side by side without an n for either, and
reads the step from 2\.47 to 2\.55
as the effect of adjusting for vascular markers; part or all of it may be the change of sample.
:::

**Outcomes.** First strokes were confirmed by CT or MRI; "In cases of fatal incidents or when
neuroimaging was unavailable, diagnosis was based on clinical evaluation and examination of medical
records". The share of events classified that way is not reported.

## Model adequacy

**Age and schooling.** The group with MMSE < 24 is 11\.5 years older at the median, with an
upper quartile of 74\.9 years against 59\.1. Adjusting
for age, gender and education leaves 60 % of
the unadjusted log hazard ratio for ischaemic stroke and
42 % for death. How age entered the
model is not stated, no coefficient other than the exposure's is reported, and diabetes, body-mass
index, lipids, smoking, alcohol, physical activity and carotid stenosis, all measured, are in no model.

::: {.evidence-inferred}
The remaining hazard ratio of about 2.5 is the whole result, and it depends on how completely a
single age term removes an eleven-year difference. The re-analysis shows the size of the dependence
([E2](#e2-the-hazard-ratio-at-equal-age-and-sex-depends-on-the-age-effect)).
:::

**Death is treated as censoring.** 7\.8 % of the group with
MMSE < 24 died during follow-up against 1\.9 % of the other.
The stroke analyses censor at death, and the curves called cumulative incidence are one minus
Kaplan–Meier.

::: {.evidence-inferred}
One minus Kaplan–Meier overstates the share with a stroke in the group that dies more. At these
event rates the overstatement is small (see the re-analysis); the point is that it was not assessed,
although the Discussion calls competing risks "non-negligible".
:::

**Fifteen exposed events.** Each of the three outcomes has 15 events
in the group with MMSE < 24. Model 2 has 9 parameters for
81 to 90 events. "The proportional hazard assumption was
met for survival analysis using the Schoenfeld residual plot method (P > 0.05)", with no statistic
and no variable named.

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
The precision of the exposure's coefficient is set by 15 events whatever the sample size. A test of
proportional hazards on 15 events detects gross departures only, and a plot has no p-value. The
adjusted estimates are fragile to the choice of covariates and of their functional forms, and the
paper shows no alternative specification.
:::

**Covariates chosen by baseline p-values.** Table 1 carries 21 tests of
group differences, none a study hypothesis, and "imbalance between groups in baseline comparisons"
is one of the two stated criteria for Model 2. Occupation, with a printed P = 0.0005 that the
printed percentages do not give (below), is in the model; diabetes is not.

## Reporting

No reporting guideline is cited. Against STROBE, the paper does not give: the time origin and time
scale of the survival analyses; the number of participants and events in each model; missing data
per covariate; how loss to follow-up was handled and how many missed each examination; the
functional form of age and homocysteine; any coefficient other than the exposure's; absolute risks.
The percentage given for missing MMSE, "about 28.8%", is the total exclusion
(1565 of 5440); the MMSE share is
27\.8 %. The analysis was not registered.
Data are "available from the corresponding author on reasonable request"; no code is available.

## Do the conclusions follow?

**"Independently forecasted."** The claim is that the association survives adjustment. The adjusted
estimate comes from a model whose sample is not stated, whose age term is not reported, and whose
exposure rests on 15 events. On the paper's own counts, the hazard ratio at equal age and sex is
between about 1.5 and 2.5 depending on an age effect that the paper leaves implicit, and its
interval includes 1 for the larger age effects
([E2](#e2-the-hazard-ratio-at-equal-age-and-sex-depends-on-the-age-effect)).

::: {.evidence-inferred}
The numbers are compatible with an association at equal age and with little or none. "Independent
predictor" is one reading among those the data allow.
:::

**"A 2.32 to 2.55 times higher risk."** A hazard ratio is read as a risk ratio. The risks, never
stated as such, are 7\.8 % against
1\.8 % for ischaemic stroke before any adjustment.

**"Cognitive screening could be valuable."** 15 of the
81 ischaemic strokes occurred in the group with MMSE < 24.

::: {.evidence-confirmed}
As a screening rule, MMSE < 24 has a sensitivity of 18\.5 %
and a positive predictive value of 7\.8 %: it misses
more than four future strokes in five. A hazard ratio does not measure screening performance, and
the paper reports no discrimination, calibration or added value over age. The recommendation has
no estimate behind it.
:::

**"But not all-cause mortality."** The mortality hazard ratio of Model 2 is
1\.79 [0\.96,
3\.36], beside
2\.32 [1\.24,
4\.36] for any stroke. The two intervals overlap almost entirely.
The difference between "forecasted" and "not" is the side of 1 on which a lower limit falls, with
15 events in each case; it is not evidence that cognition relates to stroke and not to death.

**Larger than the meta-analysis.** The effect sizes "were significantly larger than the pooled HR
of 1.19 from previous meta-analyses", with no comparison performed, and the difference is
attributed to vascular biology in Chinese populations. The paper's own attenuation from
4\.55 to 2\.47 on three
covariates points to residual confounding as the alternative it does not examine.

**Prediction and cause.** "Independently forecasted" is a prediction claim. "Cognitive impairment
is associated with an increased risk" drifts, in the Discussion's mechanisms, towards a causal one.
If low scores and later strokes share a cause in cerebrovascular disease already under way, no
adjustment for the measured covariates identifies an effect of cognition
([What the design identifies](#what-the-design-identifies)).

## Re-analysis

### Data

The authors' data were requested on 2026-11-20 and had not arrived when this was written. Everything
below runs on a reconstruction with two parts, logged in `data/derived/RECONSTRUCTION_LOG.md`.

1. **A life table.** The numbers at risk under Figure 2 give the removals per year and group; with
   Table 2 they split into strokes and deaths. The events Table 2 counts beyond those removed by
   year 4 must fall between year 4 and the end of the axis at 4.2 years. Assumptions: nobody is
   censored before year 4 (the paper reports no loss to follow-up), deaths before year 4 occur in
   people without a prior stroke, and no person carries both a stroke and a death. Event times
   within a year are unknown, so person-years are computed three ways (events spread uniformly, at
   the start, at the end of each interval); "uniform" is the main scenario.
2. **A calibrated population.** 3,875 people with the group sizes of Table 2, the sex shares of
   Table 1 and ages drawn from a distribution fitted to the Table 1 median and quartiles of each
   group, truncated at 90 years (80 and 100 as sensitivity). It carries no events: it is used to
   ask what hazard ratio at equal age and sex reproduces the Table 2 counts for a given age effect.

All results of this section are therefore *inferred*: they hold for the paper's published numbers
under the stated assumptions, and the authors' data would replace them.

### Stage 2: the paper's analysis on the reconstruction

The unadjusted Cox models refitted on the reconstructed life table return the hazard ratios of
Table 2 to within 0\.09
(@tbl-e1b, second and third columns), so the reconstruction carries the information the paper's
unadjusted analysis used. The same life table gives curves that end at
8\.0 % (MMSE < 24) and
1\.8 % (MMSE ≥ 24) for ischaemic stroke, where
Figure 2 draws 1\.00 and
0\.58 on an axis labelled cumulative incidence.

### Stages 3 and 4: the same two models, twice

Two models, each fitted by maximum likelihood (stage 3, `R/06_fit_frequentist.R`) and in Stan
(stage 4, `stan/`, `R/03_postprocess.R`), specified before fitting in `notes/04_analysis_plan.md`
and written out in [the next section](#what-this-review-fits).

- **E1**: cause-specific hazards of stroke and death, constant within each interval of the life
  table, with one group coefficient per cause; in a second structure the group coefficient has one
  value before year 4 and one after. From it: hazard ratios, cumulative incidences with death
  competing, risk differences and ratios, and the ratio of the event rate in the last 0.2 years to
  the rate before.
- **E2**: on the calibrated population, the hazard ratio for MMSE < 24 at equal age and sex that
  reproduces the two event counts of Table 2, given a hazard multiplier per decade of age. Stage 3
  fixes the age effect; stage 4 gives it one of three priors: P1 centred at 1.55 (the value at
  which the model returns the paper's Model 1 for the two stroke outcomes), P2 centred at 2
  (stroke incidence is commonly reported to double per decade of age [@kellyhayes2010]), P3 uniform
  on the log scale between 1 and 3.

Priors for stage 4: log hazard per interval Normal(log 0.005, 1.5); group coefficients Normal(0, 1),
with Normal(0, 2) as sensitivity; in E2 male sex Normal(log 1.3, 0.15).

**Sampler and fit.** 29 of 29 runs meet the thresholds set in the
plan (largest R-hat 1\.008, smallest bulk effective sample size
920, 0 divergent transitions).
310 of 310 observed counts lie inside the central 95 % of their
posterior predictive distribution. The quantities Stan generates were recomputed in R from the
parameter draws: 16 of 16 checks agree, largest difference
1e\-05. Before the data were used,
51 of 58 observed counts lay inside the prior predictive 95 %; the
exceptions are cells of the last interval and one empty cell, and the prior was kept as written.

### What the paper fits

One Cox proportional-hazards model per outcome $k \in \{$ischaemic stroke, any stroke, death$\}$
and per covariate set $z$:

$$h_k(t \mid \mathrm{CI}_i, z_i) = h_{0k}(t)\, \exp\!\big(\beta_k\, \mathrm{CI}_i + \gamma_k^{\top} z_i\big),$$

with $z$ empty (unadjusted), $z = ($age, gender, education$)$ (Model 1), and $z$ plus
homocysteine, intracranial stenosis, hypertension and occupation (Model 2). The paper reports
$\exp(\hat\beta_k)$ with a Wald interval. It does not report $h_{0k}$, which the partial
likelihood profiles out, nor any $\gamma_k$.

**What $\exp(\beta_k)$ is.** The ratio of the cause-specific hazards, the instantaneous rate of
a first event of type $k$ among people still event-free, between a person with MMSE < 24 and one
with MMSE ≥ 24 and the same $z$, assumed constant over $t$; $t$ runs from an origin the paper
does not state; the comparison is made in the participants with complete $z$ (an unstated
number for Model 2), and death is treated as independent censoring in the stroke models.

**What the paper reads it as.** "A 2.32 to 2.55 times higher risk" (Discussion). A hazard
ratio is not a risk ratio. The share of a group with a first ischaemic stroke by time $t$ is

$$F_g(t) = \int_0^{t} S_g(u)\, h_g(u)\, du, \qquad S_g(u) = \exp\!\Big(-\sum_{k'} \int_0^{u} h_{gk'}(v)\, dv\Big),$$

which needs the baseline and the death hazard the paper does not give. From the counts of
Table 2 it is 7\.8 % against 1\.8 % over the follow-up:
a risk ratio of 4\.4 and 6 more
first strokes per 100 people, before any adjustment.

**How age enters.** Presumably as $\gamma_{\text{age}}\, \text{age}_i$ on the log hazard, so
that each decade multiplies the hazard by $\theta_{\text{age}} = \exp(10\gamma_{\text{age}})$,
the same factor at 45 and at 75. With rare events the unadjusted and adjusted coefficients obey

$$\mathrm{HR}_{\text{crude}} \approx \exp(\beta_k) \times
\frac{\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(\gamma_k^{\top} z) \mid \mathrm{CI} = 1\big]}{\mathbb{E}\big[\exp(\gamma_k^{\top} z) \mid \mathrm{CI} = 0\big]},$$

the second factor being how much more hazard the exposed group carries through $z$ alone. The
paper gives the left side (4\.55) and $\exp(\hat\beta_k)$
(2\.47) and so fixes this factor at
1\.84 without saying
what $\gamma_k$ produces it, in a comparison where the groups differ by 11\.5 years at
the median. The re-analysis inverts this identity (E2 below).

**The curves.** Figure 2 draws $1 - \hat S_{gk}(t)$ with
$\hat S_{gk}(t) = \prod_{t_j \le t} (1 - d_{gkj}/n_{gj})$ and calls it cumulative incidence. With
death competing, the share with a stroke by $t$ is $F_g(t)$ above (the Aalen–Johansen estimate),
and $F_g(t) \le 1 - \hat S_{g,\text{stroke}}(t)$. On the reconstruction the gap at the end of the
axis is 0\.002
for the impaired group: negligible in size, but the label names a different quantity.

**What the p-values test.** Each answers "if $H_0$ held, how often would data at least this far
from it arise"; none estimates anything the conclusion needs.

| where | $H_0$ in symbols | was $H_0$ the question? | what the number stands in front of |
|---|---|---|---|
| Table 1, 21 rows | $F_v^{\mathrm{CI}} = F_v^{\mathrm{NCI}}$ for each baseline variable $v$ | no: two groups defined by cognition differ in age by construction; the question is by how much and what it does to $\beta_k$ | the size of each difference and its consequence; used instead to pick $z$ for Model 2 |
| Fig. 2, log-rank | $h_k^{\mathrm{CI}}(t) = h_k^{\mathrm{NCI}}(t)$ for all $t$ | no: that older, less schooled people have more strokes was not in doubt | the curves, which contradict the table |
| Methods, proportional hazards | $\beta_k(t) = \beta_k$ | a model check, legitimate in itself | with 15 exposed events the test sees gross departures only; "P > 0.05" is not evidence of proportionality |
| Table 2, interval edges | $\beta_k = 0$ at the edge | the interval is the useful part; its width is set by 15 events | — |

### What the design identifies



From the causal structure written in the plan (section 3b.4: age and sex, education, occupation, the
vascular factors measured in 2010/11, an unmeasured node U for cerebrovascular disease already under way,
and the selection S into the analysed sample), with the adjustment sets computed by dagitty rather than asserted:

- Without U, the minimal set that identifies the total effect of CI on stroke, besides S, is
  \{Age\, Sex\, Edu\, Vasc\}. Model 1 leaves the
  vascular factors open; Model 2 adds three of them and occupation, which the graph does not
  require once they are in, and is fitted on the subset with occupation recorded.
- With U, the adjustment sets are none:
  no choice of the measured covariates identifies an effect of cognition on stroke if low MMSE
  scores and later strokes share a cause in cerebrovascular disease already under way. This does
  not touch the paper's analysis; it touches its wording. "Independently forecasted" is a
  prediction claim, which U leaves intact; "cognitive impairment … heightens the risk" is a
  causal one, which U does not allow.
- Conditioning on S opens no path in this graph, but it changes the population: the estimates
  are for people who reached the 2012/13 visit event-free and completed an MMSE, and the paper
  reads them as for stroke-free adults aged 40 and over.
- Death is a competing event, not a confounder: the stroke hazard ratio is cause-specific under
  any adjustment, and the cumulative incidence needs the death hazard.
- The time origin is not a graph edge. If follow-up starts at the 2010/11 baseline while exposure
  is measured in 2012/13, the two years before the MMSE are immortal time for the exposed group.

### What this review fits

**E1, cause-specific piecewise-exponential hazards**, on the reconstructed life table. Intervals
$I_j$, $j = 1..5$: (0, 1], (1, 2], (2, 3], (3, 4], (4, 4.2]; causes $k \in \{$stroke, death$\}$;
groups $g$. In $I_j$ the hazard is constant:

$$h_{gk}(t) = \exp\!\big(\alpha_{jk} + \beta_k\, \mathrm{CI}_g\big), \quad t \in I_j; \qquad
D_{gjk} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\big(\mathrm{PY}_{gj}\, h_{gk}\big).$$

This is the paper's unadjusted Cox model with $h_{0k}$ a step function that is estimated instead of
profiled out. $\beta_k$ has the same meaning as the paper's, and because $\alpha_{jk}$ is estimated
the model also gives absolute quantities. With $S_g(t_{j-1})$ the probability of being event-free
at the start of $I_j$, $h_{g\cdot} = \sum_k h_{gk}$ and $\Delta_j = |I_j|$,

$$F_{gk}(t_j) = F_{gk}(t_{j-1}) + S_g(t_{j-1})\, \frac{h_{gk}}{h_{g\cdot}}\, \big(1 - e^{-h_{g\cdot}\Delta_j}\big),
\qquad S_g(t_j) = S_g(t_{j-1})\, e^{-h_{g\cdot}\Delta_j}.$$

Derived: $F_{gk}(4)$ and $F_{gk}(4.2)$; $\mathrm{RD}_k = F_{1k} - F_{0k}$; $\mathrm{RR}_k = F_{1k}/F_{0k}$;
the tail ratio, the hazard in $I_5$ over the person-time-weighted mean hazard in $I_1..I_4$; and,
in the second structure, $\beta_k^{(0\text{–}4)}$ and $\beta_k^{(4\text{–}4.2)}$ in place of $\beta_k$.
Stage 4 priors: $\alpha_{jk} \sim \mathrm{N}(\log 0.005, 1.5)$, $\beta \sim \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$.

Limitations: the cells come from a reconstruction; the intervals are the figure's, not chosen by
the data; $\beta_k$ is unadjusted, because the reconstruction has no covariates; a constant hazard
within a year is a coarse step; the model inherits the paper's time origin, whatever it is.

**E2, the exposure effect given an age effect**, on the calibrated population. For person $i$ with
age $a_i$ (decades from 50), sex $m_i$, group $g_i$, and follow-up $\tau = 4.1$ years:

$$\mu_i = 1 - \exp\!\big(-\tau\, \lambda_0\, e^{\,\beta_{\mathrm{CI}} \mathrm{CI}_i + \beta_{\text{age}} a_i + \beta_{m} m_i}\big),
\qquad D_g \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\Big(\sum_{i \in g} \mu_i\Big).$$

Two counts and, once $(\beta_{\text{age}}, \beta_m)$ are given, two free parameters
$(\lambda_0, \beta_{\mathrm{CI}})$: the likelihood is saturated, and $\exp(\beta_{\mathrm{CI}})$ is
the paper's Model 1 quantity, the hazard ratio between two people of the same age and sex, as a
function of $\theta_{\text{age}} = e^{\beta_{\text{age}}}$, the hazard multiplier per decade. Stage 3
fixes $\theta_{\text{age}}$ on a grid; stage 4 gives it a prior and integrates. The model adds no
information to the paper's numbers: it makes visible the assumption the adjusted estimate rests on.
Stage 4 priors: $\lambda_0 \sim \mathrm{LogN}(\log 0.004, 1.5)$, $\beta_{\mathrm{CI}} \sim \mathrm{N}(0, 1)$,
$\beta_m \sim \mathrm{N}(\log 1.3, 0.15)$; $\beta_{\text{age}} \sim \mathrm{N}(\log 1.55, 0.10)$ (P1),
$\mathrm{N}(\log 2, 0.15)$ (P2) or $\mathrm{Uniform}(0, \log 3)$ (P3).

Limitations: ages are a fitted distribution, not data; education, correlated with age, is not in
the model; sex is independent of age within group by assumption; the hazard is constant over the
follow-up.

**E3, derived from E2.** Age-equivalent $\Delta a = 10\,\beta_{\mathrm{CI}}/\beta_{\text{age}}$ years.
With $r_i$ the 4.2-year risk of person $i$, the c-index of a ranking is
$\Pr(r_i > r_j \mid i \text{ case}, j \text{ non-case})$, computed from age and sex alone and from
age, sex and MMSE status. Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values at 4.2 years come from the
same $r_i$ and a flag rule (MMSE < 24; age ≥ 65; either).

## What would settle the open points

The data request of 2026-11-20 asked for: one record per analysed participant with the MMSE score
and its date, the covariates with the visit each comes from, and the date of last contact; the date,
type and source of ascertainment of each first stroke and death; the SAS programs or listings behind
Table 1, Table 2 and Figure 2; and, if possible, the same variables for the excluded participants.
With these the time origin is read off the dates, Figure 2 is redrawn, the event dates show whether
the pile-up after year 4 is real, each model gets its n, age enters with its coefficient and a
flexible form, the continuous score replaces the cut-off, and the screening question is answered
with the measured ages. Every script in the repository runs on such a file with the reconstruction
replaced, and the evidence tags above can then be upgraded or the concerns withdrawn. Short of the
data, three numbers would settle most of it: the time origin, the n and events of Model 2, and the
age coefficient of Model 1.
